module_title: Properties of Matter and Fluid Dynamics (Intermediate)
introduction: This level shifts into fluid dynamics (fluids in motion), investigating the conservation principles governing ideal fluids, alongside real-fluid phenomena like viscosity and surface tension.

core_concepts.title: Equation of Continuity
core_concepts.description: For the streamline flow of an incompressible fluid through a pipe of varying cross-section, the product of the cross-sectional area and fluid velocity remains constant: $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$. This is based on the Conservation of Mass.

core_concepts.title: Bernoulli's Principle
core_concepts.description: For a streamline flow of an ideal fluid, the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy, and potential energy per unit volume remains constant along a streamline: $P + 0.5\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{Constant}$. This is based on the Conservation of Energy.

core_concepts.title: Viscosity & Stokes' Law
core_concepts.description: Viscosity is the internal friction force between fluid layers. Stokes' law states that the viscous drag force acting on a spherical ball of radius $r$ moving through a fluid is given by $F = 6\pi \eta r v$.

core_concepts.title: Surface Tension ($T$)
core_concepts.description: The property of a liquid surface to minimize its surface area, behaving like a stretched elastic membrane. It is measured as force per unit length: $T = F/L$.

important_entities.name: Terminal Velocity ($v_t$)
important_entities.significance: When an object falls through a viscous fluid, gravity eventually balances with the upward buoyant and viscous forces. The object then drops at a constant maximum speed (terminal velocity). This explains why raindrops don't harm us when hitting the ground.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: With an increase in temperature, the viscosity of liquids decreases, but the viscosity of gases increases. Conversely, the surface tension of liquids always decreases as temperature rises.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: According to Bernoulli's equation, if a fluid's speed ($v$) increases in a horizontal pipe, its local static pressure ($P$) must drop. This exact effect generates aerodynamic lift on an airplane's wings.

exam_strategy_tips: The excess pressure inside a hollow soap bubble is $\Delta P = 4T/R$ because it features two free surfaces (inner and outer). For a solid water droplet, it has only one free surface, making the excess pressure $2T/R$.
